meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.stem: Suppose a wage regression uses education, experience, and age (all in years) as regressors. Which of these situations would violate the classical assumption of no perfect collinearity?

options.text: Education and experience are negatively correlated in the sample (r = −0.30).
options.feedback: A correlation of −0.30 is far from an exact linear relationship. Imperfect correlation among regressors is allowed; it only makes estimates less precise.

options.text: For every worker, age equals education plus experience plus 6.
options.feedback: Correct. Age is then an exact linear function of the other two regressors, so OLS cannot separate their effects.

options.text: The sample has only 40 workers for the model's four parameters.
options.feedback: A small sample makes estimates less precise, but 40 observations still exceed four parameters, so the estimates can be computed.

options.text: Hourly wages are skewed to the right.
options.feedback: The shape of the distribution of y is not part of Assumption 3, which concerns exact linear relationships among the regressors.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.1: Assumption 3 rules out exact linear relationships among regressors. Correlated regressors are fine; an identity such as age = education + experience + 6 is not.

practice.stem: Suppose a researcher studying earnings interviews only the parents of students at her own university. Which classical assumption is most clearly in doubt?

options.text: Zero conditional mean of the error
options.feedback: This assumption is about the model's error, which is not the issue here; the problem is how the people in the data were chosen.

options.text: Linearity in the parameters
options.feedback: Linearity concerns the form of the population model, not how the observations were selected.

options.text: No perfect collinearity
options.feedback: No perfect collinearity concerns exact linear relationships among the regressors, not how the sample was drawn.

options.text: Random sampling
options.feedback: Correct. Parents of one university's students are not a random sample of the population of earners.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.1: Assumption 2 requires the data to be randomly sampled from the population of interest. A convenience sample such as one university's parents fails it.

practice.concept: Properties of the OLS estimator (Section 11.1, Key Concept 11.1)
practice.stem: Suppose Assumptions 1–4 hold for a wage regression in which the estimated return to a year of education is b<sub>educ</sub> = 1.8 dollars per hour. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Every random sample of workers would give b<sub>educ</sub> = 1.8.
options.feedback: Each sample contains different workers, so the estimate changes from sample to sample; that variation is what standard errors measure.

options.text: Across many random samples, the estimates b<sub>educ</sub> would average out to β<sub>educ</sub>.
options.feedback: Correct. That is what unbiasedness, E[b<sub>j</sub>] = β<sub>j</sub>, means.

options.text: Assumption 3 requires education to be uncorrelated with every other regressor.
options.feedback: Assumption 3 rules out only perfect (exact) collinearity. Correlated regressors are allowed.

options.text: With larger and larger samples, b<sub>educ</sub> would tend to get closer to β<sub>educ</sub>.
options.feedback: Correct. That is consistency: the estimator converges to the true value as n grows.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.1: under Assumptions 1–4, OLS is unbiased (centered on β<sub>j</sub> across samples) and consistent (closer to β<sub>j</sub> as n grows). Any single estimate still contains sampling error.

practice.concept: Interpreting a coefficient in multiple regression (Section 11.2)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression of hourly wage (dollars) on education and experience (both in years) gives predicted wage = 4.0 + 1.8 × education + 0.3 × experience. How should the 1.8 be interpreted?

options.text: Among workers with the same experience, one more year of education is associated with a $1.80 higher hourly wage, on average.
options.feedback: Correct. A multiple regression coefficient is a partial effect: the association with education holding experience fixed.

options.text: One more year of education causes every worker's hourly wage to rise by exactly $1.80.
options.feedback: The regression describes an average association in the data; it is neither causal by itself nor the same for every worker.

options.text: One more year of education is associated with a $1.80 higher hourly wage, ignoring any differences in experience between workers.
options.feedback: Ignoring experience describes a bivariate slope. In multiple regression, the other regressors are held fixed.

options.text: Workers earn $1.80 per hour for each year of education they have, on average.
options.feedback: That reads the coefficient as an average wage per year of schooling. The coefficient compares workers who differ by one year of education.

practice.explanation: Section 11.2: each coefficient is a partial effect, the expected change in y for a one-unit change in that regressor, holding the other regressors constant.

practice.concept: Standard error of a coefficient (Section 11.1, Key Concept 11.2)
practice.stem: In the formula se(b<sub>j</sub>) = s<sub>e</sub> / √(Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>²), when is Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>² small?

options.text: When the other regressors explain x<sub>j</sub> almost perfectly
options.feedback: Correct. Then little of x<sub>j</sub>'s variation is left over, Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>² is small, and se(b<sub>j</sub>) is large.

options.text: When the average value of x<sub>j</sub> is large relative to its spread
options.feedback: The level of x<sub>j</sub> does not matter; what matters is how much it varies independently of the other regressors.

options.text: When the model fits the data very well (a small s<sub>e</sub>)
options.feedback: A good fit makes s<sub>e</sub> small, the numerator. Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>² depends only on the regressors.

options.text: When the estimated coefficient b<sub>j</sub> is close to zero
options.feedback: The size of b<sub>j</sub> does not enter its standard error.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.2: when the other regressors explain x<sub>j</sub> well (multicollinearity), Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>² shrinks and se(b<sub>j</sub>) inflates.

practice.concept: Precision of coefficient estimates (Section 11.2, Key Concept 11.2)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression of wages on education, experience, and tenure is re-estimated under different conditions. Which changes would, other things equal, make se(beduc) larger? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Using a smaller sample of workers
options.feedback: Correct. Fewer observations carry less information, so the standard error rises.

options.text: Education being more highly correlated with experience and tenure
options.feedback: Correct. Less of education's variation is then independent of the other regressors, which inflates its standard error.

options.text: A larger estimated return to education
options.feedback: The size of the estimate does not enter its standard error.

options.text: Wages scattering more widely around the fitted values
options.feedback: Correct. A larger s<sub>e</sub> raises every standard error.

options.text: Testing at the 1% level instead of the 5% level
options.feedback: The significance level changes the critical value, not the standard error.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.2: se(b<sub>j</sub>) rises with a poorer fit (larger s<sub>e</sub>), a smaller sample, and less variation in x<sub>j</sub> after controlling for the other regressors (more multicollinearity).

practice.concept: Standard errors across model specifications (Sections 11.2 and 11.7)
practice.stem: Suppose adding job tenure to a wage regression raises the standard error of the experience coefficient from 0.10 to 0.25, while the coefficient itself barely changes. Tenure and experience are highly correlated (r = 0.9). What best explains the larger standard error?

options.text: Adding any regressor raises every standard error by the same proportion.
options.feedback: Standard errors change by different amounts, depending on how each regressor relates to the new one.

options.text: The sample must have become smaller when tenure was added.
options.feedback: Nothing in the scenario says observations were lost; the jump is explained by how tenure relates to experience.

options.text: Once tenure is held fixed, little independent variation in experience remains.
options.feedback: Correct. With r = 0.9, most of experience's variation is shared with tenure, so Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>² shrinks and the standard error rises.

options.text: Tenure has a larger estimated coefficient than experience in the new regression.
options.feedback: The size of another regressor's coefficient does not drive this standard error.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.2: multicollinearity shrinks the variation in x<sub>j</sub> left after controlling for the other regressors, so standard errors inflate even when the estimate barely moves.

practice.concept: Degrees of freedom and critical values (Sections 11.2–11.3)
practice.stem: Suppose two regressions use the same 30 observations: one with 2 parameters and one with 6 parameters. Their 5% two-sided t critical values are 2.048 and 2.064. Why is the second one larger?

options.text: Because the larger model leaves a smaller root MSE
options.feedback: Root MSE affects standard errors, not critical values.

options.text: Because the larger model has fewer degrees of freedom: 24 instead of 28
options.feedback: Correct. df = n − k falls from 30 − 2 = 28 to 30 − 6 = 24, and a t-distribution with fewer df has heavier tails.

options.text: Because more regressors bring the t-distribution closer to the normal
options.feedback: It works the other way: fewer df mean heavier tails.

options.text: Because the larger model tests more hypotheses at once
options.feedback: Each t critical value applies to one coefficient; the number of tests does not change it.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.1 and Section 11.3: t-statistics follow T(n − k). Each extra parameter costs one degree of freedom, and fewer df mean slightly larger critical values.

practice.stem: Suppose a salary regression reports a root MSE of $8,000. This means that actual salaries typically differ from the fitted salaries by roughly $8,000.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The root MSE s<sub>e</sub> is the standard deviation of the residuals, a typical prediction error in units of y.

options.text: False
options.feedback: The root MSE is computed from the residuals; revisit what it measures in Section 11.2.

practice.explanation: Section 11.2: root MSE s<sub>e</sub> = √(RSS/(n − k)) measures the typical size of a residual, in the units of y.

practice.concept: Constructing a confidence interval (Section 11.3, Key Concept 11.3)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression with n = 200 observations and k = 4 parameters gives b<sub>2</sub> = 5.0 with se(b<sub>2</sub>) = 2.0, and the 5% two-sided critical value is 1.972. What is the 95% confidence interval for β<sub>2</sub>?

options.feedback: This uses ± 1.972 alone. The margin of error multiplies the critical value by the standard error.
This uses ± one standard error. The margin of error is the critical value times the standard error.
This uses twice the margin of error on each side. The margin is 1.972 × 2.0 = 3.944.

practice.stem: In the same regression, b<sub>3</sub> = 7.0 with se(b<sub>3</sub>) = 2.0. Using the approximate rule b ± 2 × se, what is the approximate 95% confidence interval for β<sub>3</sub>?

options.feedback: This uses one standard error on each side; the approximate rule uses two.
A confidence interval is centered on the estimate b<sub>3</sub>, not on zero.
This uses four standard errors on each side. The rule adds and subtracts 2 × se = 4.

practice.explanation: Section 11.3: the approximate 95% interval is b ± 2 × se = 7.0 ± 4 = [3, 11]. It works well when n − k is large, as here.

practice.stem: Suppose the 95% confidence interval for the return to a year of education is [1.20, 2.40] dollars per hour. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The procedure that produced [1.20, 2.40] captures the true β<sub>educ</sub> in about 95% of repeated samples.
options.feedback: Correct. The 95% describes the long-run success rate of the procedure.

options.text: About 95% of the workers in the population earn between $1.20 and $2.40 more per hour for each year of education.
options.feedback: The interval is about one population parameter, not about individual workers.

options.text: There is a 5% chance that the interval was computed incorrectly from the sample data.
options.feedback: The 5% refers to intervals that miss β<sub>educ</sub> through sampling variation, not to computing errors.

options.text: Any value of β<sub>educ</sub> outside the interval is impossible.
options.feedback: Values outside are implausible at the 95% level, not impossible.

practice.explanation: Section 11.3: if we repeatedly sampled and built 95% intervals, about 95% would contain the true parameter. Narrower intervals mean more precise estimates.

practice.stem: Suppose the 95% confidence interval for β<sub>3</sub> is [3, 11]. For which hypothesized values would a two-sided test of H₀: β<sub>3</sub> = value be rejected at the 5% level? (Select all that apply.)

options.feedback: Correct. 0 lies outside [3, 11], so it is rejected; the coefficient is statistically significant at 5%.
10 lies inside the interval, so the data are consistent with it.
4 lies inside the interval, so it is not rejected.
Correct. 12 lies outside the interval, so it is rejected at 5%.

practice.explanation: Sections 11.3–11.4: a two-sided 5% test rejects exactly the values outside the 95% confidence interval. Values inside are consistent with the data.

practice.stem: If a coefficient's 95% confidence interval excludes zero, the 90% confidence interval from the same regression might include zero.

options.text: True
options.feedback: A 90% interval uses a smaller critical value, so it is narrower and lies inside the 95% interval; revisit Section 11.3.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The 90% interval is centered at the same estimate but is narrower, so it sits inside the 95% interval and also excludes zero.

practice.explanation: Section 11.3: all intervals share the center b<sub>j</sub>; a lower confidence level uses a smaller critical value and gives a narrower interval nested inside the wider one.

practice.stem: Suppose a policy report claims that, holding experience fixed, each additional year of education raises hourly wages by $2. Which hypotheses test this claim?

options.text: H₀: β<sub>educ</sub> = 0 vs. Hₐ: β<sub>educ</sub> ≠ 0
options.feedback: This tests whether education matters at all, not whether its effect equals $2.

options.text: H₀: b<sub>educ</sub> = 2 vs. Hₐ: b<sub>educ</sub> ≠ 2
options.feedback: Hypotheses are about the population parameter β, not the sample estimate b, which is already known.

options.text: H₀: β<sub>educ</sub> = 2 vs. Hₐ: β<sub>educ</sub> ≠ 2
options.feedback: Correct. The claimed value goes into the null hypothesis about the population coefficient.

options.text: H₀: β<sub>educ</sub> ≠ 2 vs. Hₐ: β<sub>educ</sub> = 2
options.feedback: The null hypothesis is the specific value being tested; the not-equal sign belongs in the alternative.

practice.explanation: Section 11.4: a two-sided test of a specific value is H₀: β<sub>j</sub> = β<sub>j</sub>* vs. Hₐ: β<sub>j</sub> ≠ β<sub>j</sub>*, here with β<sub>j</sub>* = 2.

practice.stem: In the regression with b<sub>3</sub> = 7.0 and se(b<sub>3</sub>) = 2.0, what is the t-statistic for H₀: β<sub>3</sub> = 10?

options.feedback: This is b<sub>3</sub>/se, the statistic for H₀: β<sub>3</sub> = 0. Subtract the hypothesized value 10 first.
This divides the hypothesized value by the standard error; the estimate must enter the numerator.
The subtraction order is reversed. The numerator is estimate minus hypothesized value: 7.0 − 10 = −3.0.

practice.explanation: Section 11.4: t = (b<sub>j</sub> − β<sub>j</sub>*)/se(b<sub>j</sub>) = (7.0 − 10)/2.0 = −1.50. With |t| = 1.50 below 1.972, H₀ is not rejected at 5%.

practice.stem: Suppose the p-value for H₀: β<sub>exper</sub> = 0 in a wage regression is 0.003. What does it mean?

options.text: The probability that β<sub>exper</sub> equals zero, given these data, is 0.003.
options.feedback: A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true; it is not the probability that H₀ is true.

options.text: Under H₀: β<sub>exper</sub> = 0, results at least as extreme as this one would occur in roughly 0.3% of samples.
options.feedback: Correct. That is the definition of a p-value.

options.text: Wages rise with experience for 99.7% of the workers in the population being studied.
options.feedback: The p-value concerns the estimate's sampling distribution, not the share of workers with any property.

options.text: There is a 0.3% chance that the estimate was computed with an error.
options.feedback: The p-value measures sampling variation under H₀, not computational mistakes.

practice.explanation: Section 11.4: the p-value is the probability, if H₀ were true, of an estimate at least as extreme as the one observed. Reject H₀ when p < α.

practice.stem: In the regression with b<sub>2</sub> = 5.0 and se(b<sub>2</sub>) = 2.0, the 5% two-sided critical value is 1.972. What is the correct conclusion about H₀: β<sub>2</sub> = 0?

options.text: Do not reject H₀, because 5.0 lies inside its own 95% confidence interval.
options.feedback: Every confidence interval contains its own estimate. What matters is whether the interval contains 0.

options.text: Reject H₀, because 5.0 is larger than the critical value 1.972.
options.feedback: The critical value is compared with the t-statistic, not with the coefficient, whose size depends on units.

options.text: Do not reject H₀, because the standard error 2.0 is larger than 1.972.
options.feedback: The standard error is not compared with the critical value; the ratio b/se is.

options.text: Reject H₀, because t = 5.0/2.0 = 2.5 is larger than 1.972.
options.feedback: Correct. |t| = 2.5 > 1.972, so x<sub>2</sub> is statistically significant at 5%.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.4: t = b<sub>j</sub>/se(b<sub>j</sub>) = 2.5. Reject H₀: β<sub>j</sub> = 0 when |t| exceeds the critical value, equivalently when p < α.

practice.concept: What a test of significance examines (Section 11.4, Key Concept 11.4)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression of wages on education and experience. What does the test of H₀: β<sub>exper</sub> = 0 examine?

options.text: Whether experience and wages are correlated in the sample, ignoring education
options.feedback: A simple correlation ignores education. The coefficient in a multiple regression holds education fixed.

options.text: Whether every worker's wage rises with experience
options.feedback: The coefficient describes an average partial relationship, not every individual worker.

options.text: Whether experience is related to wages once education is held fixed
options.feedback: Correct. The test concerns the partial effect of experience after controlling for education.

options.text: Whether the intercept of the regression is zero
options.feedback: The intercept is β<sub>1</sub>; this test concerns the experience coefficient.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.4: H₀: β<sub>j</sub> = 0 asks whether x<sub>j</sub> has any partial effect on y after controlling for the other regressors.

practice.stem: Suppose the tenure coefficient in a wage regression is 0.8 with a p-value of 0.40. Then the 95% confidence interval for β<sub>tenure</sub> includes zero.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. A two-sided 5% test fails to reject β = 0 exactly when 0 lies inside the 95% interval, and p = 0.40 > 0.05.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the link between two-sided tests and confidence intervals (Sections 11.3–11.4).

practice.explanation: Sections 11.3–11.4: p = 0.40 > 0.05 means H₀: β<sub>tenure</sub> = 0 is not rejected at 5%, so 0 lies inside the 95% interval. That is a lack of evidence, not proof that the effect is zero.

practice.stem: Suppose two regressors each have individual p-values around 0.15. Why can a joint F-test of both still reject H₀ that both coefficients are zero?

options.text: Because the two estimates can be correlated, which a joint F-test takes into account
options.feedback: Correct. The joint test uses how the two estimates move together.

options.text: Because p-values add up, so the joint p-value is 0.15 + 0.15 = 0.30 in this case
options.feedback: Joint p-values are not sums of individual ones; they come from the F distribution.

options.text: Because an F-test always rejects when two or more regressors are tested at once
options.feedback: An F-test can fail to reject; the chapter's own subset test does.

options.text: Because individual p-values use robust standard errors and F-tests do not
options.feedback: Both can be computed with classical or robust standard errors; that is not the reason.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.5: a joint F-test evaluates both restrictions at once, so regressors that are individually insignificant can still be jointly significant, especially when they are correlated.

practice.stem: Consider y = β<sub>1</sub> + β<sub>2</sub>x<sub>2</sub> + β<sub>3</sub>x<sub>3</sub> + β<sub>4</sub>x<sub>4</sub> + β<sub>5</sub>x<sub>5</sub> + β<sub>6</sub>x<sub>6</sub> + u. To test whether only x<sub>2</sub> and x<sub>3</sub> belong in the model, how many restrictions (q) does H₀ impose?

options.feedback: 2 is the number of regressors that stay in the model. Count the coefficients set to zero.
5 is the number of slope coefficients. Only those of x<sub>4</sub>, x<sub>5</sub>, and x<sub>6</sub> are restricted.
Correct. H₀: β<sub>4</sub> = β<sub>5</sub> = β<sub>6</sub> = 0 has three restrictions.
6 is the number of parameters in the model. Count only the restrictions under H₀.

practice.explanation: Section 11.5: the number of restrictions q is the number of equations in H₀; here β<sub>4</sub> = 0, β<sub>5</sub> = 0, and β<sub>6</sub> = 0, so q = 3.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of test scores on four school characteristics, using 60 schools, gives an overall F-statistic of 1.20 with p = 0.32. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each of the four characteristics has been shown to have no effect on test scores.
options.feedback: Failing to reject is not proof that the effects are zero; the data simply cannot rule out zero.

options.text: At the 5% level, we cannot reject H₀ that all four slope coefficients are zero.
options.feedback: Correct: p = 0.32 > 0.05.

options.text: The result is also not significant at the 10% level.
options.feedback: Correct: p = 0.32 > 0.10.

options.text: The probability that all four slope coefficients are zero is 0.32.
options.feedback: A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true; it is not the probability that H₀ is true.

options.text: Explained variation per restriction is only slightly larger than unexplained variation per degree of freedom.
options.feedback: Correct. F = 1.20 is that ratio, only a little above 1.

practice.explanation: Sections 11.5–11.6: the overall F-test asks whether all slopes are zero. F = 1.20 (p = 0.32) gives no evidence against H₀ at 5% or 10%, which is different from proving that the regressors are irrelevant.

practice.concept: The F distribution and its degrees of freedom (Section 11.5)
practice.stem: In the six-parameter model above, estimated with n = 100, H₀ restricts the coefficients of x<sub>4</sub>, x<sub>5</sub>, and x<sub>6</sub> to zero. Which distribution does the F-statistic follow under H₀?

options.feedback: 97 = n − 3 is the restricted model's degrees of freedom. The denominator uses the unrestricted model's n − k.
5 counts all slopes. The numerator degrees of freedom equal the number of restrictions.
Correct: q = 3 restrictions and n − k = 100 − 6 = 94.
The order is reversed: restrictions first, then n − k.

practice.explanation: Section 11.5: F ~ F(q, n − k), with q = 3 restrictions and n − k = 100 − 6 = 94 from the unrestricted model.

practice.stem: The 5% critical value of an F distribution depends on both its numerator and its denominator degrees of freedom.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The F distribution is indexed by two degrees of freedom, and its critical values change with each.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the F-distribution properties listed in Section 11.5.

practice.explanation: Section 11.5: F(q, n − k) depends on two parameters, the number of restrictions and the residual degrees of freedom, so critical values change with both.

practice.concept: Restricted and unrestricted models (Section 11.6, Key Concept 11.7)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression of wages on education, experience, tenure, and union membership. To test H₀: β<sub>tenure</sub> = β<sub>union</sub> = 0, which is the restricted model?

options.text: Wages on tenure and union membership only
options.feedback: This keeps exactly the variables whose coefficients H₀ sets to zero.

options.text: Wages on education and experience
options.feedback: Correct. The restricted model imposes H₀ by dropping tenure and union membership.

options.text: Wages on education, experience, tenure, and union membership
options.feedback: This is the unrestricted model; it imposes no restriction.

options.text: Wages on education only
options.feedback: This also drops experience, which H₀ does not restrict.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.7: the restricted model imposes H₀ (here, it omits tenure and union membership); the unrestricted model keeps all regressors.

practice.stem: Suppose two models are estimated on n = 53 observations: a restricted model with k<sub>r</sub> = 3 and RSS<sub>r</sub> = 40, and an unrestricted model with k<sub>u</sub> = 6 and RSS<sub>u</sub> = 30. What is the F-statistic?

options.feedback: This is the formula upside down. The increase in RSS per restriction goes in the numerator.
This forgets to divide the increase in RSS by q = 3.
This uses n − k<sub>r</sub> = 50; the denominator uses the unrestricted model's n − k<sub>u</sub> = 47.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.6: F = [(RSS<sub>r</sub> − RSS<sub>u</sub>)/q] / [RSS<sub>u</sub>/(n − k)] with q = 6 − 3 = 3 and n − k = 47, giving 5.22, above the 5% critical value of F(3, 47), about 2.80.

practice.stem: A larger F-statistic means that the restrictions being tested fit the data better.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what a large increase in RSS says about the restrictions (Key Concept 11.6).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. A large F means imposing the restrictions raises RSS a lot, so the restrictions are inconsistent with the data.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.6: larger F-values indicate that the restricted model fits much worse, which is evidence against the restrictions.

practice.concept: Testing a subset of regressors (Section 11.6, Key Concept 11.7)
practice.stem: Suppose an F-test of whether three extra regressors can be dropped from a model gives p = 0.01. Which conclusion is correct at the 5% level?

options.text: Reject H₀: at least one of the three coefficients is nonzero.
options.feedback: Correct. p = 0.01 < 0.05, so the restrictions are rejected.

options.text: All three coefficients are shown to be nonzero in the population.
options.feedback: Rejecting a joint null says at least one restriction fails, not that every coefficient is nonzero.

options.text: The probability that all three coefficients are zero is 0.01.
options.feedback: A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true; it is not the probability that H₀ is true.

options.text: Each of the three regressors is individually significant at 5%.
options.feedback: A joint test says nothing directly about individual t-tests; some or all could be individually insignificant.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.7: a small p-value in a subset F-test means the extra regressors are jointly significant; the restricted (simpler) model fits significantly worse.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression has TSS = 500 and RSS = 200. Then the regressors explain 40% of the variation in y.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit how TSS splits into ESS and RSS (Section 11.6).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. ESS = 500 − 200 = 300, so the regressors explain 300/500 = 60%; RSS is the 40% left unexplained.

practice.explanation: Section 11.6: TSS = ESS + RSS, so ESS = 300 and R² = ESS/TSS = 0.60. RSS/TSS = 0.40 is the unexplained share.

practice.stem: Suppose a coefficient in a regression table has p = 0.07. Under the asterisk convention of Section 11.7, how is it marked?

options.feedback: Three asterisks are reserved for p < 0.01.
Correct: one asterisk marks 0.05 ≤ p < 0.10.
Two asterisks mark p < 0.05; 0.07 is above that.

options.text: No asterisk
options.feedback: p = 0.07 is below 0.10, which earns one asterisk.

practice.explanation: Section 11.7: *** for p < 0.01, ** for p < 0.05, * for p < 0.10. A p-value of 0.07 is significant at 10% but not at 5%.

practice.stem: Suppose three nested wage models estimated on n = 40 workers, with one, two, and three regressors (Models 1, 2, and 3), have R² of 0.300, 0.330, and 0.335 and adjusted R² of 0.282, 0.294, and 0.280. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Model 2 has the highest adjusted R².
options.feedback: Correct: 0.294 is the largest adjusted R².

options.text: Model 3 is best because it has the highest R².
options.feedback: R² never falls when a regressor is added, so the largest model always wins on R².

options.text: Adjusted R² can never fall when a regressor is added.
options.feedback: Model 3 shows the opposite: adjusted R² falls from 0.294 to 0.280 because of the complexity penalty.

options.text: Model 3's higher R² shows that its extra regressor is statistically significant.
options.feedback: A small rise in R² can be pure chance; significance requires a test.

options.text: Because R² never falls when a regressor is added, R² alone cannot choose among these models.
options.feedback: Correct. That is why adjusted R² or F-tests are used to compare them.

practice.explanation: Section 11.7: compare nested models with adjusted R² or F-tests rather than with raw R²; here Model 2 has the best adjusted R².

practice.stem: In a typical model comparison table, what appears in parentheses below each coefficient unless the table note says otherwise?

options.text: The p-value of the model's overall F-test
options.feedback: The overall F and its p-value are reported once per model, at the bottom of the column.

options.text: The model's R²
options.feedback: Fit statistics such as R² appear at the bottom of each column, not under each coefficient.

options.text: The coefficient's standard error
options.feedback: Correct. Standard errors in parentheses are the most common default; the note should still say so.

options.text: The number of observations
options.feedback: N is reported once per model at the bottom of the table.

practice.explanation: Section 11.7: tables usually report standard errors in parentheses beneath the coefficients and say so in a note; fit statistics are reported once per model.

practice.stem: Suppose a wage regression is re-estimated with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The coefficient estimates do not change.
options.feedback: Correct. Only the standard errors are computed differently.

options.text: The t-statistics and p-values can change.
options.feedback: Correct. They depend on the standard errors.

options.text: The robust standard errors are valid whether or not the error variance is constant.
options.feedback: Correct. That is their purpose.

options.text: Robust standard errors are always smaller than classical ones.
options.feedback: Robust standard errors can be larger or smaller than classical ones; there is no fixed direction.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.8: HC1 standard errors leave the coefficients unchanged and give valid inference without assuming constant error variance; t-statistics and p-values change with them.

practice.stem: Robust standard errors are needed only when the sample has fewer than 30 observations.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what robust standard errors protect against (Key Concept 11.8).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Robust standard errors address non-constant error variance, which can occur at any sample size.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 11.8: heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors guard against non-constant error variance, not against small samples; reporting them is best practice for cross-sectional data.

exam.stem: Which of the following would violate the classical assumption of no perfect collinearity in the Davis regression of price on size, bedrooms, bathrooms, lot size, age, and month sold?

options.text: Including age and month sold, which are moderately correlated in the sample (r = −0.37)
options.feedback: Revisit what kind of relationship among regressors Assumption 3 rules out (Section 11.1).

options.text: Estimating seven parameters with a sample of only 29 houses
options.feedback: Revisit whether sample size is part of Assumption 3 (Section 11.1).

options.text: Adding each house's size in square meters alongside its size in square feet
options.feedback: Correct. Square meters are an exact multiple of square feet, an exact linear relationship among regressors.

options.text: Including lot size, which takes only three distinct values in the data
options.feedback: Revisit what kind of relationship among regressors Assumption 3 rules out (Section 11.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.1: Assumption 3 rules out exact linear relationships among regressors. Size in square meters is size in square feet times a constant, so OLS could not separate the two.

exam.stem: Suppose neighborhood quality, which is not among the regressors in the Davis regression, raises house prices and tends to be higher where houses are larger. Which classical assumption would this violate?

options.text: Zero conditional mean of the error
options.feedback: Correct. Neighborhood quality sits in the error u, and it varies with size, so E[u | size, …] would not be zero.

options.text: No perfect collinearity
options.feedback: Revisit what each of Assumptions 1–4 requires (Key Concept 11.1).

options.text: Random sampling
options.feedback: Revisit what each of Assumptions 1–4 requires (Key Concept 11.1).

options.text: Linearity of the model in its parameters
options.feedback: Revisit what each of Assumptions 1–4 requires (Key Concept 11.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.1: Assumption 4 requires E[u | x<sub>2</sub>, …, x<sub>k</sub>] = 0. An omitted factor that affects price and moves with size violates it.

exam.concept: Properties of the OLS estimator (Section 11.1, Key Concept 11.1)
exam.stem: In the Davis full model, the size coefficient is b<sub>size</sub> = 68.37. If Assumptions 1–4 hold, which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: b<sub>size</sub> is an unbiased estimator: its sampling distribution has mean β<sub>size</sub>.
options.feedback: Correct. That is unbiasedness: E[b<sub>size</sub>] = β<sub>size</sub>.

options.text: The estimate 68.37 equals β<sub>size</sub> exactly.
options.feedback: Revisit the difference between an estimate and the population parameter (Section 11.1).

options.text: As the number of houses grows without limit, b<sub>size</sub> converges to β<sub>size</sub>.
options.feedback: Correct. That is consistency.

options.text: OLS has a smaller variance than any other estimator of β<sub>size</sub>, linear or not.
options.feedback: Revisit the class of estimators the Gauss-Markov theorem compares (Section 11.1).

options.text: The six regressors are uncorrelated with one another.
options.feedback: Revisit what Assumption 3 does and does not require (Section 11.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.1: under Assumptions 1–4, OLS is unbiased and consistent. Any single estimate still has sampling error, BLUE compares only linear unbiased estimators, and regressors may be correlated as long as they are not perfectly collinear.

exam.concept: Interpreting a coefficient in multiple regression (Section 11.2)
exam.stem: In the Davis full model, the coefficient on size is 68.37 (price in dollars, size in square feet). Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Each additional square foot causes the price of every house to rise by $68.37, whatever its other features.
options.feedback: Revisit how the chapter words the meaning of a regression coefficient (Section 11.2).

options.text: The average price per square foot of the 29 houses is $68.37.
options.feedback: Revisit how a slope coefficient differs from an average ratio (Section 11.2).

options.text: One more square foot is associated with a $68.37 higher price on average, ignoring differences in the other five regressors.
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 11.2 interprets each coefficient in a multiple regression.

options.text: Holding the other five regressors fixed, one more square foot is associated with a $68.37 higher price, on average.
options.feedback: Correct. It is a partial effect, holding the other regressors constant.

exam.explanation: Section 11.2: each coefficient is a partial effect. Holding the other five regressors constant, one more square foot is associated with a $68.37 higher price on average.

exam.concept: Standard error of a coefficient (Section 11.1, Key Concept 11.2)
exam.stem: In the formula se(b<sub>j</sub>) = s<sub>e</sub> / √(Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>²), what is x̃<sub>ji</sub>?

options.text: The deviation of x<sub>ji</sub> from the sample mean of x<sub>j</sub>
options.feedback: Revisit how x̃<sub>ji</sub> is defined in Section 11.1.

options.text: The residual from regressing x<sub>j</sub> on all the other regressors
options.feedback: Correct. It is the part of x<sub>j</sub> that the other regressors do not explain.

options.text: The residual from regressing y on all the regressors
options.feedback: Revisit how x̃<sub>ji</sub> is defined in Section 11.1.

options.text: The fitted value from regressing x<sub>j</sub> on all the other regressors
options.feedback: Revisit how x̃<sub>ji</sub> is defined in Section 11.1.

exam.explanation: Section 11.1: x̃<sub>ji</sub> is the residual from regressing x<sub>j</sub> on the other regressors, so Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>² measures the variation in x<sub>j</sub> that is not shared with them.

exam.concept: Precision of coefficient estimates (Section 11.2, Key Concept 11.2)
exam.stem: For the Davis full model, which changes would, other things equal, make the standard error of the size coefficient smaller? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Testing H₀: β<sub>size</sub> = 50 instead of H₀: β<sub>size</sub> = 0
options.feedback: Revisit the ingredients of se(b<sub>j</sub>) in Key Concept 11.2.

options.text: Data on more houses from the same market
options.feedback: Correct. A larger sample carries more information about the coefficient.

options.text: Sampling houses with a wider range of sizes
options.feedback: Correct. More variation in size gives more information about its coefficient.

options.text: Reporting a 99% instead of a 95% confidence interval
options.feedback: Revisit the difference between a standard error and a confidence level (Sections 11.2–11.3).

options.text: Prices lying closer to the fitted values (a smaller s<sub>e</sub>)
options.feedback: Correct. A better-fitting model gives more precise coefficients.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.2: se(b<sub>j</sub>) = s<sub>e</sub>/√(Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>²) falls with a better fit, a larger sample, and more variation in x<sub>j</sub>. The estimate's size and the confidence level do not enter it.

exam.concept: Standard errors across model specifications (Sections 11.2 and 11.7)
exam.stem: Using the same 29 houses, the standard error of the size coefficient is 11.17 when size is the only regressor and 15.39 in the full model, while the coefficient moves from 73.77 to 68.37. What is the main reason the standard error is larger in the full model?

options.text: The size coefficient is smaller in the full model, and smaller coefficients have larger standard errors.
options.feedback: Revisit the ingredients of se(b<sub>j</sub>) in Key Concept 11.2.

options.text: Size is correlated with the added regressors, so less of its own variation remains once they are held fixed.
options.feedback: Correct. That shrinks Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>² and inflates the standard error.

options.text: The full model reports heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors instead of classical ones.
options.feedback: Revisit which standard errors the chapter's model comparison reports (Section 11.7).

options.text: Adding regressors always lowers the root MSE, which raises the standard errors.
options.feedback: Revisit how s<sub>e</sub> enters se(b<sub>j</sub>), and how it behaves when regressors are added (Section 11.2).

exam.explanation: Sections 11.2 and 11.7: size is correlated with the other regressors (for example, r = 0.52 with bedrooms), so controlling for them leaves less independent variation in size. Σ x̃<sub>ji</sub>² shrinks and se rises from 11.17 to 15.39.

exam.stem: For the same 29 houses, the 5% two-sided t critical value is 2.052 in the regression of price on size alone but 2.074 in the full model. Why is it larger in the full model?

options.text: Because the full model's standard errors are larger than the size-only model's
options.feedback: Revisit what determines a critical value of the t-distribution (Sections 11.3–11.4).

options.text: Because the full model has a higher R² than the size-only model
options.feedback: Revisit what determines a critical value of the t-distribution (Sections 11.3–11.4).

options.text: Because the full model uses a higher confidence level for its intervals
options.feedback: Revisit what determines a critical value of the t-distribution (Sections 11.3–11.4).

options.text: Because it estimates more parameters, leaving fewer degrees of freedom
options.feedback: Correct. More parameters mean fewer degrees of freedom and a t-distribution with heavier tails.

exam.explanation: The t-statistic follows T(n − k). The full model estimates k = 7 parameters, leaving 22 degrees of freedom instead of 27, so its critical value is slightly larger.

exam.stem: In the Davis full model, the root MSE of about $24,936 measures how much the size coefficient would typically vary from one sample of houses to another.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what the root MSE measures and in what units (Section 11.2).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The root MSE is the typical size of a residual, in dollars of price; the sampling variation of the size coefficient is its standard error, 15.39.

exam.explanation: Section 11.2: root MSE s<sub>e</sub> is the standard deviation of the residuals, a typical prediction error of about $24,936. The standard error of a coefficient measures how much that estimate varies across samples.

exam.concept: Constructing a confidence interval (Section 11.3, Key Concept 11.3)
exam.stem: In the Davis full model, b<sub>size</sub> = 68.37 with se(b<sub>size</sub>) = 15.39, and the t critical value for a 90% confidence interval is 1.717. What is the 90% confidence interval for β<sub>size</sub>?

options.feedback: Revisit the margin-of-error formula in Key Concept 11.3 and recompute it step by step.
Revisit the margin-of-error formula in Key Concept 11.3 and recompute it step by step.
Revisit the margin-of-error formula in Key Concept 11.3 and recompute it step by step.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.3: b<sub>j</sub> ± t<sub>crit</sub> × se(b<sub>j</sub>) = 68.37 ± 1.717 × 15.39 = 68.37 ± 26.42 = [41.95, 94.79], narrower than the 95% interval.

exam.stem: In the Davis full model, the bedrooms coefficient is 2,685 with a standard error of 9,193. Using the approximate rule b ± 2 × se, what is the approximate 95% confidence interval for β<sub>bedrooms</sub>?

options.feedback: Revisit the approximate 95% rule in Section 11.3.
Revisit the approximate 95% rule in Section 11.3.
Revisit the approximate 95% rule in Section 11.3.

exam.explanation: Section 11.3: 2,685 ± 2 × 9,193 = [−15,701, 21,071]. The exact interval with 2.074 is a bit wider, and both contain zero.

exam.stem: The 95% confidence interval for β<sub>size</sub> in the Davis full model is [36.45, 100.29] dollars per square foot. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: About 95% of the 29 houses sold for between $36.45 and $100.29 per square foot.
options.feedback: Revisit what the interval is about: a population parameter or individual houses (Section 11.3).

options.text: There is a 95% chance that the sample estimate b<sub>size</sub>, computed from these 29 houses, lies between 36.45 and 100.29.
options.feedback: Revisit which quantity is fixed and which is random in the interpretation of Section 11.3.

options.text: If many samples of 29 houses were drawn and such an interval built from each, about 95% would contain β<sub>size</sub>.
options.feedback: Correct. The 95% is the long-run success rate of the procedure.

options.text: The true β<sub>size</sub> equals 68.37 with 95% probability.
options.feedback: Revisit the interpretation of a confidence interval in Section 11.3.

exam.explanation: Section 11.3: if we repeatedly sampled 29 houses and built 95% intervals, about 95% of them would contain the true β<sub>size</sub>. Every value in [36.45, 100.29] is positive.

exam.stem: The 95% confidence interval for β<sub>size</sub> is [36.45, 100.29]. For which hypothesized values would a two-sided test of H₀: β<sub>size</sub> = value be rejected at the 5% level? (Select all that apply.)

options.feedback: Correct. 30 lies outside the interval.
Revisit how a 95% interval relates to a two-sided 5% test (Sections 11.3–11.4).
Correct. 0 lies outside the interval, so size is statistically significant at 5%.
Correct. 105 lies outside the interval.
Revisit how a 95% interval relates to a two-sided 5% test (Sections 11.3–11.4).

exam.explanation: Sections 11.3–11.4: a two-sided 5% test rejects exactly the values outside the 95% interval: 0, 30, and 105. The values 60 and 100 lie inside (100 only just: |t| = 2.06 < 2.074).

exam.stem: For any coefficient in the Davis full model whose 95% confidence interval contains zero, the 99% confidence interval from the same regression also contains zero.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The 99% interval has the same center and a larger critical value, so it contains the whole 95% interval.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit how the critical value changes with the confidence level (Section 11.3).

exam.explanation: Section 11.3: higher confidence means a larger critical value and a wider interval around the same estimate, so a 99% interval contains the 95% interval.

exam.stem: Suppose a real-estate agent claims that, holding the other regressors fixed, each additional year of age lowers a house's price by $1,000. The Davis estimate is b<sub>age</sub> = −833. Which hypotheses test the agent's claim?

options.text: H₀: β<sub>age</sub> = 0 vs. Hₐ: β<sub>age</sub> ≠ 0
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 11.4 states the null and alternative hypotheses.

options.text: H₀: β<sub>age</sub> = −1,000 vs. Hₐ: β<sub>age</sub> ≠ −1,000
options.feedback: Correct. The claimed value goes into H₀ about the population coefficient.

options.text: H₀: β<sub>age</sub> = 1,000 vs. Hₐ: β<sub>age</sub> ≠ 1,000
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 11.4 states the null and alternative hypotheses.

options.text: H₀: β<sub>age</sub> = −833 vs. Hₐ: β<sub>age</sub> ≠ −833
options.feedback: Revisit how Section 11.4 states the null and alternative hypotheses.

exam.explanation: Section 11.4: H₀: β<sub>j</sub> = β<sub>j</sub>* vs. Hₐ: β<sub>j</sub> ≠ β<sub>j</sub>*, with β<sub>j</sub>* = −1,000, the agent's claim. Hypotheses concern the population β, not the estimate.

exam.stem: In the Davis full model, b<sub>size</sub> = 68.37 with se(b<sub>size</sub>) = 15.39. What is the t-statistic for H₀: β<sub>size</sub> = 50?

options.feedback: Revisit how the t-statistic is formed from the estimate and its standard error (Section 11.4).
Revisit how the t-statistic is formed from the estimate and its standard error (Section 11.4).
Revisit how the t-statistic is formed from the estimate and its standard error (Section 11.4).

exam.explanation: Section 11.4: t = (b<sub>j</sub> − β<sub>j</sub>*)/se(b<sub>j</sub>) = (68.37 − 50)/15.39 = 1.19, below 2.074, so H₀: β<sub>size</sub> = 50 is not rejected at 5%.

exam.stem: In the Davis full model, b<sub>size</sub> = 68.37 and the p-value for H₀: β<sub>size</sub> = 0 is 0.0002. What does the p-value mean?

options.text: If β<sub>size</sub> were zero, an estimate this far or farther from zero would occur in only about 2 of 10,000 samples.
options.feedback: Correct. That is the definition of a p-value.

options.text: The probability that β<sub>size</sub> equals zero, given the data on these 29 houses, is 0.0002.
options.feedback: Revisit what a p-value assumes and what it measures (Section 11.4).

options.text: The probability that 68.37 is the true value of β<sub>size</sub> is 0.9998.
options.feedback: Revisit what a p-value assumes and what it measures (Section 11.4).

options.text: Only 0.02% of the variation in house prices is left unexplained by the regression once size is included.
options.feedback: Revisit the difference between a p-value and a measure of fit (Sections 11.2 and 11.4).

exam.explanation: Section 11.4: the p-value is the probability, if H₀ were true, of an estimate at least as extreme as the one observed: about 2 in 10,000 here, so H₀ is rejected decisively.

exam.stem: In the Davis full model, the age coefficient is −833 with a standard error of 719, and the 5% two-sided critical value is 2.074. Which conclusion about H₀: β<sub>age</sub> = 0 is correct?

options.text: Do not reject H₀ at 5%: the estimate is less than 2.074 standard errors from zero.
Reject H₀ at 5%: the estimate is negative, so older houses sell for less.
options.feedback: Revisit what the decision rule compares (Key Concept 11.4).

options.text: Reject H₀ at 5%: the coefficient's magnitude, 833, is far larger than the critical value 2.074.
options.feedback: Revisit what the decision rule compares (Key Concept 11.4).

options.text: Do not reject H₀ at 5%: an $833 effect is too small to matter economically.
options.feedback: Revisit the difference between economic and statistical significance (Section 11.7 and Common Mistakes to Avoid).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.4: t = −833/719 = −1.16 and |t| < 2.074, so age is not statistically significant at 5%. The decision compares |t|, not the coefficient, with the critical value.

exam.concept: What a test of significance examines (Section 11.4, Key Concept 11.4)
exam.stem: In the Davis full model, what does the test of H₀: β<sub>bathrooms</sub> = 0 examine?

options.text: Whether bathrooms and price are correlated across the 29 houses, ignoring the other regressors
options.feedback: Revisit what the test of statistical significance examines in a multiple regression (Key Concept 11.4).

options.text: Whether bathrooms and size are unrelated across the 29 houses
options.feedback: Revisit what the test of statistical significance examines in a multiple regression (Key Concept 11.4).

options.text: Whether bathrooms is related to price once the other five regressors are held fixed
options.feedback: Correct. The test concerns the partial effect of bathrooms.

options.text: Whether the effect of bathrooms is large in dollar terms
options.feedback: Revisit the difference between statistical and economic significance (Section 11.7 and Common Mistakes to Avoid).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.4: H₀: β<sub>j</sub> = 0 asks whether x<sub>j</sub> has any partial effect on y after controlling for the other regressors.

exam.stem: In the Davis full model, the bedrooms coefficient has p = 0.773, which shows that the number of bedrooms has no effect on house prices.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what failing to reject H₀ does and does not establish (Section 11.4).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Failing to reject is not proof that the effect is zero; the estimate is imprecise (se = 9,193), and bedrooms is positively correlated with price (r = 0.43).

exam.explanation: Section 11.4: failing to reject H₀ is not the same as proving H₀ true. Bedrooms adds little once size is controlled for, but its wide interval is consistent with both zero and sizable effects.

exam.stem: Why does the chapter test the five regressors other than size jointly with an F-test instead of reading off their five separate t-tests?

options.text: Because a joint test always rejects when at least one of the five coefficients is individually significant
options.feedback: Revisit the motivation for joint tests in Key Concept 11.5.

options.text: Because separate t-tests ignore correlation between the estimates and cannot test the five restrictions jointly
options.feedback: Correct. The F-test evaluates the restrictions jointly and accounts for that correlation.

options.text: Because F-tests do not need the residuals or the standard errors of the regression
options.feedback: Revisit how the F-statistic is computed (Section 11.6).

options.text: Because running several separate t-tests makes each of the five coefficient estimates less precise
options.feedback: Revisit the motivation for joint tests in Key Concept 11.5.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.5: individual t-tests cannot test multiple restrictions simultaneously because they ignore correlations between coefficient estimates; the F-test compares the restricted and unrestricted fits.

exam.stem: In the Davis full model, how many restrictions (q) does H₀: β<sub>lotsize</sub> = β<sub>age</sub> = 0 and β<sub>bedrooms</sub> = β<sub>bathrooms</sub> impose?

options.feedback: Revisit how restrictions are counted (Section 11.5).
Revisit how restrictions are counted (Section 11.5).
Revisit how restrictions are counted (Section 11.5).
Correct: β<sub>lotsize</sub> = 0, β<sub>age</sub> = 0, and β<sub>bedrooms</sub> − β<sub>bathrooms</sub> = 0.

exam.explanation: Section 11.5: q counts the separate equations in H₀. Two coefficients set to zero plus one equality between two coefficients gives q = 3, even though four coefficients appear.

exam.stem: For the Davis full model, the test of overall significance gives F = 6.83 with p = 0.0003. Which conclusions are justified? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At least one regressor has a nonzero slope coefficient in the population.
options.feedback: Correct. Rejecting H₀ that all slopes are zero means at least one is not.

options.text: Each of the six regressors has a nonzero partial effect on price in the population.
options.feedback: Revisit what the alternative hypothesis of the overall F-test states (Section 11.5).

options.text: The probability that all the slope coefficients are zero is 0.0003.
options.feedback: Revisit what a p-value assumes and what it measures (Section 11.4).

options.text: The F-test by itself does not reveal which regressors drive the result.
options.feedback: Correct. Identifying which regressors matter requires the individual t-tests.

exam.explanation: Section 11.5: F = 6.83 (p = 0.0003) rejects H₀: β<sub>2</sub> = ⋯ = β<sub>7</sub> = 0, so at least one slope is nonzero. The test does not say which; the individual t-tests point to size.

exam.concept: The F distribution and its degrees of freedom (Section 11.5)
exam.stem: The Davis full model regresses price on six regressors plus an intercept, using 29 houses. Under H₀, which distribution does the overall F-statistic follow?

options.feedback: Revisit what the numerator degrees of freedom count (Section 11.5).
Revisit the order of the two degrees of freedom in F(q, n − k) (Section 11.5).
Revisit how the denominator degrees of freedom are computed (Section 11.5).
Correct: q = 6 slope restrictions and n − k = 29 − 7 = 22.

exam.explanation: Section 11.5: F ~ F(q, n − k). The overall test restricts the six slopes (q = k − 1 = 6) and the model estimates k = 7 parameters, so n − k = 22.

exam.stem: Like a t-statistic, an F-statistic can take negative values.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the properties of the F distribution listed in Section 11.5.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. F is a ratio of nonnegative quantities (an RSS increase and an RSS), so it is never negative.

exam.explanation: Section 11.5: the F distribution is always positive and right-skewed. Imposing restrictions can never lower the RSS, so the numerator of F is never negative.

exam.concept: Restricted and unrestricted models (Section 11.6, Key Concept 11.7)
exam.stem: To test H₀: β<sub>bedrooms</sub> = β<sub>bathrooms</sub> = 0 in the Davis full model, which model is the restricted model?

options.text: Price on bedrooms and bathrooms, with no other regressors
options.feedback: Revisit how the restricted model imposes H₀ (Key Concept 11.7).

options.text: Price on all six regressors
options.feedback: Revisit how the restricted model imposes H₀ (Key Concept 11.7).

options.text: Price on size, lot size, age, and month sold
options.feedback: Correct. It imposes H₀ by dropping bedrooms and bathrooms.

options.text: Price on size only
options.feedback: Revisit which coefficients this H₀ restricts (Key Concept 11.7).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.7: the restricted model imposes H₀, here by omitting bedrooms and bathrooms; the unrestricted model keeps all six regressors.

exam.stem: The chapter tests H₀ that the coefficients of bedrooms, bathrooms, lot size, age, and month sold are all zero. The restricted model has RSS = 14,975 million; the unrestricted model has RSS = 13,679 million and estimates 7 parameters from the 29 houses. What is the F-statistic?

options.feedback: Revisit each part of the F formula in Key Concept 11.6.
Revisit each part of the F formula in Key Concept 11.6.
Revisit each part of the F formula in Key Concept 11.6.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.6: F = [(RSS<sub>r</sub> − RSS<sub>u</sub>)/q] / [RSS<sub>u</sub>/(n − k)] with q = 5 and n − k = 29 − 7 = 22: (1,296/5)/621.8 = 0.42, far below the 5% critical value of 2.66.

exam.concept: The F-statistic in terms of R² (Section 11.6, Key Concept 11.6)
exam.stem: If adding a set of regressors to a model left R² exactly unchanged, the F-statistic for testing those regressors would equal 1.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the R² form of the F-statistic in Key Concept 11.6 and evaluate its numerator.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. With R²<sub>u</sub> = R²<sub>r</sub>, the numerator (R²<sub>u</sub> − R²<sub>r</sub>)/q is zero, so F = 0.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.6: F = [(R²<sub>u</sub> − R²<sub>r</sub>)/q] / [(1 − R²<sub>u</sub>)/(n − k)]. No gain in R² means F = 0, no evidence at all against the restrictions.

exam.concept: Testing a subset of regressors (Section 11.6, Key Concept 11.7)
exam.stem: The F-test of whether bedrooms, bathrooms, lot size, age, and month sold can be dropped from the Davis full model gives p = 0.83. Which conclusion is correct at the 5% level?

options.text: The probability that all five coefficients are zero is 0.83.
options.feedback: Revisit what a p-value assumes and what it measures (Section 11.4).

options.text: The five are not jointly significant at 5%; dropping them does not significantly worsen the fit.
options.feedback: Correct. p = 0.83 > 0.05, so the restrictions are not rejected.

options.text: At least one of the five regressors has a nonzero coefficient in the population.
options.feedback: Revisit the decision rule for an F-test (Key Concept 11.7).

options.text: The test proves that bedrooms, bathrooms, lot size, age, and month sold have no effect on price.
options.feedback: Revisit what failing to reject H₀ establishes (Section 11.4).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.7: a small F with a large p-value (0.83) means the extra regressors do not significantly improve fit, so the simpler model is preferred, without proving their effects are exactly zero.

exam.stem: Going from the size-only model to the full model lowers RSS and raises ESS but leaves TSS unchanged.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. TSS depends only on price, so adding regressors just shifts variation from RSS to ESS.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit how TSS splits into ESS and RSS (Section 11.6).

exam.explanation: Section 11.6: TSS = Σ(y − ȳ)² depends only on price; adding regressors moves variation from RSS (14,975 → 13,679 million) to ESS.

exam.stem: Under the asterisk convention of Section 11.7, how is the intercept of the Davis full model, with p = 0.035, marked?

options.feedback: Revisit the thresholds of the asterisk convention (Section 11.7).
Revisit the thresholds of the asterisk convention (Section 11.7).
Correct: 0.01 ≤ 0.035 < 0.05 earns two asterisks.

options.text: No asterisk
options.feedback: Revisit the thresholds of the asterisk convention (Section 11.7).

exam.explanation: Section 11.7: *** for p < 0.01, ** for p < 0.05, * for p < 0.10. A p-value of 0.035 is significant at 5% but not at 1%.

exam.stem: The chapter compares Model 1 (size), Model 2 (size and bedrooms), and Model 3 (all six regressors). Their R² values are 0.617, 0.618, and 0.651; their adjusted R² values are 0.603, 0.589, and 0.555. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Model 1 has the highest adjusted R² even though it has the lowest R².
options.feedback: Correct: 0.603 is the largest adjusted R², while 0.617 is the smallest R².

options.text: R² cannot fall when regressors are added, so its rise to 0.651 alone does not show that Model 3 is better.
options.feedback: Correct. R² mechanically rises (or stays the same) as regressors are added.

options.text: Model 2 has a larger residual sum of squares than Model 1, since its adjusted R² is lower.
options.feedback: Revisit how R² and adjusted R² differ (Section 11.7).

options.text: Adjusted R² can fall when a regressor is added, because it penalizes model complexity.
options.feedback: Correct. That is why it falls from 0.603 to 0.589 to 0.555.

exam.explanation: Section 11.7: R² never falls when regressors are added; adjusted R² penalizes complexity and here favors Model 1. Model 2 actually has a slightly higher R² (lower RSS) than Model 1.

exam.stem: Section 11.7 shows Models 1–3 side by side in one comparison table. What is the main advantage of this layout?

options.text: It shows which of the three models gives the causal effect of size on price.
options.feedback: Revisit the purpose of a model comparison table (Section 11.7).

options.text: It makes each model's standard errors smaller than in separate regression outputs.
options.feedback: Revisit the purpose of a model comparison table (Section 11.7).

options.text: It lets readers skip the standard errors, because R² summarizes each model's uncertainty.
options.feedback: Revisit the purpose of a model comparison table (Section 11.7).

options.text: It shows how the size estimate and its precision change across models.
options.feedback: Correct. Here the size coefficient moves from 73.77 to 72.41 to 68.37 while its standard error rises.

exam.explanation: Section 11.7: putting specifications side by side lets readers see how coefficient estimates and their standard errors change across specifications, alongside fit statistics such as R², N, and F.

exam.stem: The chapter re-estimates the Davis full model with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. The standard error of the size coefficient changes from 15.39 to 15.36, and that of the intercept from 61,465 to 65,545. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The t-statistic for size falls noticeably under robust standard errors.
options.feedback: Revisit how t is formed from the estimate and its standard error (Section 11.4).

options.text: The coefficient estimates are identical to those of the classical regression.
options.feedback: Correct. HC1 changes only the standard errors.

options.text: Robust standard errors are valid only if the error variance is the same for every house.
options.feedback: Revisit what heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are designed for (Key Concept 11.8).

options.text: The size coefficient remains statistically significant at the 1% level.
options.feedback: Correct. Its robust p-value is still about 0.0002.

options.text: The intercept's standard error changes by a larger percentage than the size coefficient's.
options.feedback: Correct: about +6.6% for the intercept versus −0.2% for size.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 11.8: HC1 leaves the coefficients unchanged and changes the standard errors in either direction (size: 15.39 → 15.36, so t goes from 4.44 to 4.45; intercept: 61,465 → 65,545, about +6.6%). Size stays significant at 1%.

exam.stem: For the Davis full model, switching from classical to robust standard errors does not change which coefficients are statistically significant at the 5% level.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The intercept and size are significant at 5% under both; the other five regressors are not significant under either.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the comparison of classical and robust results in Section 11.7.

exam.explanation: Section 11.7: the intercept (p = 0.035 classical, 0.047 robust) and size (p ≈ 0.0002) are significant at 5% either way; the other coefficients stay insignificant, so the conclusions are robust.
